why:
The chapter defines the word directly in Sec. 6.2: when an external force acts on a body it produces a change in the size or the shape of the body, and that change in dimensions is called deformation. So the term the blank is asking for is *deformation*.

Why the others fail. *Formation* is not a term this chapter uses at all — it is the opposite idea, the making of a body rather than a change in one already made. *Contraction* names only ONE kind of dimensional change, a decrease in size; a wire that is stretched also changes its dimensions, and calling that a contraction would be wrong, so the word is too narrow to be the general name. *Strain* is not the change in dimensions but the RATIO of that change to the original dimension — Sec. 6.3 defines strain as change in dimension divided by original dimension, which makes it a dimensionless number rather than the change itself. Strain is what you compute FROM the deformation, so it cannot be another name for it.

Read the stress-strain curve of Sec. 6.6 from the origin. Along OA stress and strain rise together in proportion — this is the region where Hooke's law holds, and A is the proportional limit. A little beyond it lies the elastic limit, up to which the wire still returns to its original length when unloaded. Past that comes the point where the material begins to yield: the strain goes on increasing even though the stress is not increased any further, and the deformation stops being reversible. That point is called the *yield point*.

Why the others fail. The *elastic point* (elastic limit) is where reversibility ends, but the strain does not run away there — stress must still be raised to raise the strain further, which is exactly the behaviour the stem excludes. The *breaking point* is the far end of the curve, where the wire actually fractures; nothing increases beyond it because the specimen no longer exists. The *neck point* refers to the local thinning that develops well after yielding, in the plastic region near fracture, and is not the point at which the runaway strain first sets in.

Strain energy per unit volume is the total strain energy divided by the volume, so the volume is the total energy divided by the energy density:

\(V = \dfrac{\text{strain energy}}{\text{strain energy per unit volume}} = \dfrac{18 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}}{6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J/m}^{3}} = 3\ \text{m}^{3}\)

The units settle it as much as the arithmetic: dividing joules by joules-per-cubic-metre leaves cubic metres, so the answer must be quoted in m\(^{3}\), and the value is 3.

Why the others fail. The pair 3 cm\(^{3}\) and 6 cm\(^{3}\) carry the wrong unit — the energy density is given per cubic METRE, and 3 cm\(^{3}\) is \(3 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{3}\), a million times too small; it would hold only \(1.8 \times 10^{-8}\) J. The value 6 m\(^{3}\) comes from dividing the wrong way round or from doubling instead of dividing — checked against the data, 6 m\(^{3}\) at \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) J/m\(^{3}\) would store \(36 \times 10^{-3}\) J, twice the energy the question states.

Sec. 6.8 opens with this sentence word for word: hardness is the property of a material which enables it to resist plastic deformation. The stem is a verbatim quotation of the book's own definition, so the blank is *hardness*. The section adds that hardness also covers resistance to bending, scratching, abrasion or cutting, and that the greater the hardness the greater the resistance to deformation.

Why the others fail. *Elasticity* is the property of regaining the original shape once the deforming force is removed — it concerns recoverable, ELASTIC deformation, whereas the stem asks about resisting PLASTIC deformation, which by definition is not recovered. *Plasticity* is the exact opposite of what is wanted: a plastic material retains the deformed shape, so plasticity permits plastic deformation rather than resisting it. *Ductility* is the ability to be drawn into wires, which the chapter associates with metals having a LARGE plastic range — a ductile material undergoes a great deal of plastic deformation before breaking, again the reverse of resisting it. Sec. 6.8 makes that contrast explicitly: hard materials have little ductility.

Sec. 6.8 states it in these words: toughness is the ability of a material to resist fracturing when a force is applied to it. The stem quotes that definition verbatim, so the property being named is *toughness*. The book illustrates it with plasticine clay, which is relatively tough because it can be stretched and deformed by an applied force without breaking.

Why the others fail. The same section warns that hardness of a material is different from its strength and its toughness, and defines *hardness* as resistance to plastic DEFORMATION, not to fracture — diamond is the standard example of a hard material and is also brittle, so it is hard and not tough, which is precisely the pair the book separates. *Elasticity* is the ability to regain the original shape after the deforming force is removed; a glass rod is highly elastic within its limit and yet shatters readily, so elasticity says nothing about resistance to fracture. *Plasticity* is the tendency to retain a deformed shape, a different property again, and the chapter's own example of a tough substance (plasticine) shows the two are not interchangeable, since what makes it tough is that it deforms WITHOUT breaking rather than that it stays deformed.
